candidates.title: Functionalization of AFM Tips and Supports for Molecular Recognition Force Spectroscopy and Recognition Imaging.
candidates.authors: Ebner A, Wildling L, Gruber HJ
candidates.abstract: Linking sensor molecules (e.g., antibodies) to an AFM tip converts it into a biosensor by which single target molecules (e.g., antigens) can be detected and localized on the sample surface. Moreover, the mechanism of interaction can be studied by force spectroscopy if purified target molecules are linked to an ultra-flat surface, such as mica or silicon (nitride). Rapid imaging of the binding sites and force spectroscopy studies are greatly facilitated if 6-10 nm long polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains are used as flexible tethers between the sensor molecule and the tip. Here, we describe a set of methods by which a variety of proteins, oligonucleotides, or small molecules can be tethered to silicon (nitride) tips or to mica. Methods are included which afford site-specific and oriented coupling of the sensor molecules.

candidates.title: mRNA-LNP delivery of a homo-tandem nanobody protects goslings from novel goose astrovirus infection.
candidates.authors: Wang D, Shao X, Ai Y, et al.
candidates.abstract: Novel goose astrovirus (nGAstV) infection causes visceral gout and high mortality in goslings, but at present, there are no effective vaccines or antiviral agents. Here, we identified a neutralizing nanobody (Nb60) targeting the spike (P2) protein of nGAstV capable of inhibiting viral replication by blocking both viral attachment and entry. For effective in vivo delivery, we designed an mRNA-encoded homo-tandem nanobody (3×Nb60) flanked by an Anser interleukin-2 (IL-2) signal peptide and Anser untranslated regions that exhibited an approximately twofold improvement in neutralization potency compared to the mRNA-encoded Nb60 monomer. The mRNA encoding nanobody was encapsulated with lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to prolong its half-life in serum by approximately 48 h. In a gosling infection model, the 3×Nb60 mRNA-LNP (2 mg/kg) produced 100% survival for both prophylaxis and therapy, significantly reduced viral shedding and viral loads in tissues, attenuated hepatic and renal pathology, and restored serum uric acid, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase levels to close to the baseline values. Epitope mapping revealed that Nb60 recognizes a critical conformational epitope on the P2 protein, with residues 529R and 553G being essential for binding. The findings establish an mRNA-encoded nanobody platform as a promising strategy for prophylaxis and therapy in the early stages of nGAstV infection.IMPORTANCENovel goose astrovirus (nGAstV) has caused widespread outbreaks of visceral gout in goslings across China since 2017, leading to substantial economic losses in the poultry industry. The disease predominantly affects goslings under 3 weeks of age, and the short disease course limits the utility of conventional vaccines. This study establishes an mRNA-encoded nanobody (Nb) platform in which avian-specific regulatory elements, including an Anser IL-2 signal peptide and an Anser globin untranslated region, enable efficient expression of a neutralizing Nb60 in avian cells. A homo-tandem design (3×Nb60) further prolongs the in vivo half-life, improves antiviral potency, and provides complete protection in goslings. By offering a species-matched delivery framework, this platform provides a rapid-response strategy for emerging avian viral diseases and may also shed light on the development of mRNA-encoded antibody therapeutics against human enteric viruses.

candidates.title: Phase 1 durability study of a single dose of the live-attenuated cholera vaccine PanChol and the safety and immunogenicity of a second dose
candidates.authors: Leitner, D. R., Walsh, S. R., Sherman, A. C., et al.
candidates.abstract: Background Killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccines require multiple doses and have reduced efficacy in young children, limiting their utility. PanChol is a single-dose, oral live-attenuated cholera vaccine engineered from a current seventh pandemic El Tor O1 Vibrio cholerae strain. PanChol was shown to be safe and immunogenic in a previous phase 1a trial. In participants from this first-in-human trial, we aimed to assess the durability of the initial PanChol dose and the safety and immunogenicity of a second dose. Methods This open-label phase 1a booster study was conducted at Brigham and Women's Hospital (Boston, MA). Eligible participants were healthy adults aged 18-55 years without a history of cholera or gastrointestinal disorders and had received a PanChol dose ranging from 105-1010 colony-forming units (CFU) within the previous 322-1111 days. All participants received a booster dose of 2x107 CFU. The primary outcome was safety, including solicited, unsolicited, and serious adverse events following the second dose of PanChol. Secondary endpoints were the magnitude of pre- and post-vaccination serum vibriocidal titers to both Inaba and Ogawa V. cholerae, including seroconversion (4-fold rise in titers over baseline), and stool shedding of PanChol organisms using quantitative and qualitative stool cultures. Comparisons of the amount of vaccine shedding in stool following primary and secondary immunization were used to assess the intestinal mucosal immunity elicited by the initial PanChol dose. All outcomes were assessed in all participants. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05657782, and is complete. Findings Between Aug 25, 2025, and Feb 20, 2026, 20 healthy adults who previously received a single oral dose of PanChol were enrolled to receive a booster dose of 2x107 CFU. Eleven (55%) of 20 participants were male and the median age was 43{middle dot}6 (IQR 30{middle dot}2-49{middle dot}5). Ten (50%) were White and 17 (85%) were not Hispanic or Latino. Nine (45%) of 20 boost recipients reported at least one solicited adverse event; 13 (93%) of 14 events were mild, and all were transient. The most common solicited adverse event was nausea, reported by 4 (20%) participants; all cases were mild. Most unsolicited adverse events were mild; one was grade 3 and was deemed unrelated to vaccination. Two unsolicited adverse events were deemed related to vaccination (mild gassy sensation and heartburn, both of which occurred on day 1 and resolved the same day). In most participants, vibriocidal antibody titers measured on the day of boosting exceeded baseline titers prior to the initial dose (17 (85%) for Inaba and 14 (70%) for Ogawa). Fifteen (75%) of 20 boost recipients seroconverted vibriocidal antibody titers to both serotypes. After the boost, 17 (85%) participants had no or self-limited vaccine shedding, compared with 10% after the first PanChol dose. Interpretation A second oral dose of PanChol had a favorable safety profile and induced vibriocidal seroconversion to both serotypes in 75% of boost recipients. Intestinal colonization of PanChol following the boost serves as a proxy for measuring mucosal immunity targeting V. cholerae. The decrease in in the abundance of PanChol fecal shedding following the second dose, compared with the first, suggests that a single dose of PanChol is sufficient to confer durable protective immunity against a cholera challenge. These observations underscore the need for further clinical development of PanChol. Funding Wellcome Trust.

candidates.title: Orthogonal Fc engineering enables multiplexed delivery of mRNA-encoded bispecific antibodies that constrain viral escape.
candidates.authors: Wec AZ, Cho A, Pecetta S, et al.
candidates.abstract: The continuous antigenic evolution of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has repeatedly undermined the effectiveness of monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapies, underscoring the need for innovative approaches that improve therapeutic mAb breadth and durability of protection. Here, we engineered messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA)-encoded bispecific antibodies (bsAbs) that, upon intravenous administration in lipid nanoparticles, achieved high serum concentrations, extended half-life, and serum neutralizing titers exceeding 1:10,000 in human neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)-expressing mice. To enhance resilience to viral escape, we used structure-guided computational design to introduce Fc modifications that promoted selective homodimerization, thereby enabling codelivery of multiple mRNA-encoded bsAbs with cognate heavy chain pairing. In vivo expression of a triple bsAb combination resulted in broad serum neutralization of historical and contemporary SARS-CoV-2 variants, including the highly mutated BA.3.2.2 lineage. Preexposure prophylaxis with the mRNA-delivered bsAb combination conferred protection against SARS-CoV-2 XBB.1.5 challenge, preventing weight loss and decreasing viral burden in the lungs compared with vehicle control treatment. Together, the results provide proof of principle for mRNA-based delivery of Fc-engineered bsAb combinations to combat SARS-CoV-2 and potentially other rapidly evolving pathogens.

candidates.title: Microfluidic Extraction of Extracellular Vesicle-Associated Nucleic Acids for Downstream Molecular Analysis
candidates.authors: Lage, T., Macedo, D., Silva, H. I., et al.
candidates.abstract: Aim: To develop a microfluidic workflow for extracting extracellular vesicle (EV)-associated nucleic acids (NAs) from biofluids, such as blood plasma and serum, for downstream molecular analysis. Methods: Healthy serum and plasma samples were spiked with EVs obtained from Hec-1-A cells carrying defined mutations and characterized in accordance with MISEV guidelines. The spiked samples were then processed using either the standard centrifugation-based ExoGAG protocol or a microfluidic workflow. The latter combines ExoGAG mediated aggregation of EVs with mechanical entrapment of the resulting EV aggregates in a microfluidic filtration device (EVNA-chip). The retained material was washed and on-chip lysed to release its NA cargo. NAs were subsequently purified using a commercial silica column, producing an output suitable for molecular analysis through droplet digital PCR (ddPCR). Results: The EVNA-chip recovery yield was 42.0 +/- 4.28% and 38.1 +/- 1.46% for double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) and microRNA respectively. The recovered dsDNA remained compatible with ddPCR detection of the KRAS p.G12D variant (c.35G>A) and with the assessment of MSI-associated alterations using BAT25, BAT26, NR21, NR24, and MONO27. The method was demonstrated for pilot cohort of patients with endometrial cancer. The RNA workflow supported reverse transcription and was demonstrated for the quantification of miR-X, a potential marker of Fabry disease, using patient samples and healthy controls. Conclusion: Although recovery was lower than with the standard protocol (~45% for DNA and for RNA), the centrifugation-free EVNA-chip workflow demonstrates the compatibility of the method with downstream NA molecular analyses and is advantageous for the development of an integrated, automated platform for EV-based liquid biopsy applications.

candidates.title: Lateral flow devices can fast-track rabies virus genomic surveillance
candidates.authors: Crisostomo, B., Bautista, C., Miranda, M. E., et al.
candidates.abstract: Viral genomic data can resolve rabies transmission and guide outbreak response, but surveillance is often limited less by sequencing capacity than by getting suitable specimens from remote collection sites to a laboratory, a process that can take months. Here, we show that lateral flow devices (LFDs) used for rabies diagnosis can also serve as genomic specimens, integrating diagnosis and genomic sampling into a single workflow without additional specimen collection. We evaluated LFDs and FTA cards for rabies virus genome recovery under laboratory and field conditions. During surveillance across the island provinces of MIMAROPA, Philippines, the Bionote LFD had 99.1% sensitivity and 100% specificity against the gold-standard direct fluorescent antibody test (n = 319), with results available a median of 1 day after sampling versus 5 days for DFAT confirmation. Under laboratory conditions simulating field storage (ambient temperature or 37 degrees Celsius for up to 21 days), both residual LFD material and FTA cards supported near-complete genome sequencing, although genome recovery declined with storage duration, particularly at elevated temperatures. Consistent with this, field-collected LFDs yielded near-complete genomes up to 23 days of ambient storage but only partial genomes after 29-77 days, indicating a practical window of around three weeks for use. Repurposing LFDs already embedded in diagnostic workflows offers a practical route to decentralised genomic surveillance without additional sample collection or a cold chain. FTA cards provide a complementary preservation option, while further optimisation of specimen preparation, extraction and storage could improve genome recovery and extend the sequencing window.

candidates.title: Human-Guided Agentic AI for End-to-End EHR Research: Sequential Antibody-Drug Conjugate Pathways in Breast Cancer
candidates.authors: Loaiza-Bonilla, A., Colovos, C., Kim, D., et al.
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To demonstrate an end-to-end research workflow combining a large electronic health record (EHR) resource and a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) system governed by Human-Guided Orchestration (HGO), using sequential sacituzumab govitecan (SG) and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) orders in breast cancer as the clinical use case. METHODS: A June 2026 EHR release contained 4.95 million patients, including 156,051 with breast cancer codes. Muse Spark supported cohort construction, executable statistical analysis, data-quality checks, literature retrieval, and reporting executed through Symbiotic Agent Teaming (SAT) under investigator direction. The main clinical measure was the second-drug record span, from first to last order. Analyses were descriptive and unadjusted; orders did not confirm administration or progression. RESULTS: The workflow identified 106 patients: 73 had T-DXd ordered first and 33 had SG ordered first. Median second-drug spans were 63 days (interquartile range [IQR], 29-116) for SG after T-DXd and 49 days (IQR, 21-126) for T-DXd after SG; the median difference was -14 days (95% bootstrap CI, -41 to 21; distributional P = 0.42). Reported outputs additionally included cohort definitions, aggregate analyses, evidence context, figures, and a preliminary draft manuscript. CONCLUSION: This study provides a concrete model for integrating large EHR resources, agentic AI, and human expertise across the research cycle. The ADC use case illustrates how computational execution and Expert-in-the-Loop (EITL) adjudication can produce interpretable research outputs and refine their scientific meaning, providing a foundation for extending and evaluating this approach across clinical questions.

candidates.title: Hierarchical embolization integrating hypoxia modulation and immune reprogramming for enhanced hepatocellular carcinoma therapy.
candidates.authors: Zhang C, Wu H, Xing E, et al.
candidates.abstract: Transarterial embolization (TAE) remains a primary treatment option for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, but its efficacy is often compromised by incomplete vascular occlusion and treatment resistance caused by hypoxia. Conventional embolic agents suffer from poor distal embolization due to particle-vessel size mismatch, while the resulting hypoxia microenvironment aggravates chemoresistance and fosters immune-suppression. To overcome these challenges, we developed a hierarchical embolization system based on the mSiO2/Pt/aPD-1@HAMA microspheres that synergistically enhance vascular occlusion and therapeutic response. In this system, hyaluronic acid methacryloyl (HAMA) microspheres achieve the proximal arterial embolization, whereas mesoporous silica (mSiO2) particles embedded within the HAMA matrix are sized to correspond to vessels of capillary caliber and are designed to achieve secondary microvascular occlusion after release, with the aim of establishing a multi-level hierarchical vascular embolization. In addition, the Pt nanoparticles loaded in mSiO2 catalyze the decomposition of tumor-overexpressed H2O2 into O2, partially alleviating hypoxia and disrupting resistance mechanisms within the tumor microenvironment. Importantly, instead of conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy in transcatheter arterial chemoembolization (TACE), this hierarchical embolic system incorporates anti-PD-1 (aPD-1) antibodies within the mesoporous channels of mSiO2, thereby directing the local therapeutic action toward immune activation. Synergistically, the oxygen-enriched microenvironment induced by Pt-catalysis further augments the immune checkpoint blockade by reversing local immunosuppression and restoring T cell function. In a preclinical rabbit VX2 tumor model, this hierarchical embolization strategy achieved markedly enhanced anti-tumor effect compared with standard embolic agents. Collectively, these findings provide proof-of-concept evidence for an embolization strategy integrating hierarchical vascular occlusion, hypoxia modulation, and immune checkpoint blockade.

candidates.title: Engineered cells that sense and respond to interleukin-23 with neutralizing therapy for autoimmunity
candidates.authors: Garza, G. L., Danon, S. N. L., Wuchter, J., et al.
candidates.abstract: Engineered cell sensors are powerful tools for monitoring biomarkers and delivering timely therapy. Here we create an engineered cell sensor of interleukin-23 (IL-23), a critical biomarker in many autoimmune diseases, and a therapeutic delivery platform for autoimmune disease management. We utilized Modular Extracellular Sensor Architecture (MESA), a promising platform given its modularity and previously developed cell sensors for immune targets such as IL-10. First, we developed a library of IL-23 MESA receptors by incorporating IL-23-specific nanobody binders and performed high-throughput functional screening. We achieved further receptor optimization by modifying the extracellular linker length and the ratio of receptor chain expression. Receptor performance was highly correlated with predicted geometric features such as binder pair distance and degree of transmembrane domain dimerization. The receptors were limited by poor surface expression and functioned most effectively as sensors for intracellular IL-23. Finally, we modified the IL-23 sensing circuit to output an IL-23 neutralizing nanobody with the potential to reduce inflammation triggered by IL-23 secretion. This sense-and-respond architecture can be utilized for dynamic therapeutic treatment to meet the dynamic relapse-remitting pattern of many autoimmune diseases.

candidates.title: Thermoplastic polyurethane as a base material for soft, high-density neural interfaces
candidates.authors: Pak, A., Velea, A. I., Hosman, T., et al.
candidates.abstract: Polymers used as substrate and encapsulation for implantable devices are typically deposited layer-by-layer, leaving polymer-polymer interfaces that adhere poorly and become a critical failure point. Thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) elastomers combine four properties not found together in any other candidate: decades of clinical use in long-term implants and availability in medical grade, a stiffness well below that of polyimide and parylene C, compatibility with microfabrication, and thermoplastic self-fusion, which removes the polymer-polymer interface entirely. This work introduces TPU as a base material for soft, high-density neural interfaces and demonstrates one route to realizing them. Gold is patterned on a sacrificial copper sheet by maskless lithography and transferred into TPU by vacuum lamination, giving conformally coated tracks down to 15 um at 30 um pitch within a single, merged polymer body. An additional electroplating step produces a nanostructured pinecone gold surface that increases the electrochemically active area of the electrodes, approximately doubling the charge injection capacity. Daisy-chain silicon chips were also embedded within the soft polymer body. The films transmit up to 88% at 470 nm, a wavelength commonly used for optogenetics. TPU showed no cytotoxicity towards differentiated SH-SY5Y cells and only a mild tissue response after 9.5 months of subcutaneous implantation in rats.

candidates.title: RNA evidence supports clinical stage antibody drug targets in oncology
candidates.authors: Pozzobon, D., Khusial, N., Spreafico, R., et al.
candidates.abstract: Background: The selection of efficacious and safe antibody-based oncology targets depends on tumor specificity and normal-tissue expression, and remains challenging. Bulk RNA-seq can identify tumor-enriched surface genes, but may obscure tumor specificity and normal-cell expression patterns that are relevant to the therapeutic window. We evaluated whether single-cell RNA-seq-derived expression features improve retrospective prioritization of clinically pursued antibody targets. Methods: We developed a bulk and single-cell RNA expression-based ranking framework across six solid tumor indications. 4,532 candidate surfaceome targets were scored using tumor Specificity, normal Safety, and blood Sink features derived from bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, or a combined modality. Ranking performance was evaluated against a curated validation set of tumor-associated antibody-based oncology targets using logistic regression, with odds ratios (ORs) reported per one-standard-deviation increase in score. Results: Higher Specificity scores were associated with clinical-stage target selection across all modalities. In cross-indication meta-analysis, single-cell Specificity showed higher ORs than bulk Specificity across clinical phase thresholds, including Phase [≥] 1 (OR 2.56 versus 1.81), Phase [≥] 2 (OR 2.77 versus 1.88), Phase [≥] 3 (OR 3.53 versus 2.04) and Approved targets (OR 3.51 versus 1.74). Combined bulk-and-single-cell Specificity showed intermediate enrichment. Specificity score alone did not consistently show a significant single-cell advantage over bulk in paired indication-level comparisons, except for Phase [≥] 3 targets. After adding normal-cell Safety and blood Sink features, the single-cell general score showed the strongest enrichment across thresholds (Phase [≥] 1 OR 3.61, Phase [≥] 2 OR 4.16, Phase [≥] 3 OR 5.57, and Approved targets OR 4.25). This general score also showed consistently significant single-cell advantage over bulk in paired indication-level comparisons. Safety contributed most strongly in the single-cell modality, increasing meta-analytic ORs by an average of ~36% across thresholds compared to Specificity alone. Performance varied by indication, with breast cancer showing weaker Specificity-based enrichment. Conclusion: Expression-derived ranking features are retrospectively enriched among clinically pursued tumor-associated antibody targets. Single-cell evidence is most informative when tumor Specificity is combined with normal-cell Safety information, supporting its use as an interpretable component of early antibody target prioritization. These findings are in alignment with recent evidence that single-cell RNA-based cell-type specificity supports clinical-stage targets and demonstrate that expression-driven ranking can systematically recover clinically relevant oncology targets.

candidates.title: Inhibition of CDK1 attenuates cardiac remodeling via suppression of fibroblast-derived TGF-β1.
candidates.authors: Yamamoto T, Matsushima S, Noda E, et al.
candidates.abstract: Activation of cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) is implicated in fibrosis in liver and skin. However, the role of CDK1 in cardiac remodeling remains unclear. We investigated whether CDK1 inhibition suppresses cardiac remodeling and explored the underlying mechanisms. Angiotensin II (Ang II) was continuously infused into C57BL/6 mice with or without intraperitoneal administration of a selective CDK1 inhibitor (Ro-3306) for 1 week. Ro-3306 attenuated Ang II-induced increases in left ventricular wall thickness and heart weight without affecting blood pressure. Ro-3306 also ameliorated interstitial fibrosis and cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in Ang II-treated hearts, accompanied by reduced Col1a1 and Col3a1 mRNA expression. Ang II increased phosphorylation of CDK1 substrate motifs and transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) precursor protein levels, a key mediator of cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy, and these were suppressed by Ro-3306. Ro-3306 also attenuated pressure overload-induced cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy, accompanied by reduced TGF-β1 precursor protein levels. In cultured cardiac fibroblasts, inhibition of CDK1 by Ro-3306 or small interfering RNA suppressed Ang II-induced increases in TGF-β1 precursor protein levels, whereas no such effect was observed in cultured cardiomyocytes. In contrast, CDK2 knockdown or CDK4/6 inhibitors did not affect TGF-β1 precursor protein levels in cardiac fibroblasts. Comprehensive secretome analysis identified TGF-β1 as a major growth factor secreted from fibroblasts in response to Ang II. Conditioned medium from fibroblasts treated with Ang II induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. CDK1 knockdown in fibroblasts suppressed TGF-β1 secretion. Neutralizing TGF-β1 antibodies attenuated hypertrophic effects of conditioned medium from fibroblasts treated with Ang II. In conclusion, CDK1 inhibition attenuates cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy in vivo, accompanied by reduced cardiac TGF-β1 precursor protein levels. Our in vitro findings further suggest that CDK1 in cardiac fibroblasts regulates TGF-β1 production and secretion, thereby contributing to cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. KEYWORDS: CDK1 Cardiac fibrosis Cardiac hypertrophy TGF-β1.

candidates.title: Development of a highly sensitive photometric readout platform technology using SPAAC-modified HRP liposomes.
candidates.authors: Dobner C, Hoecherl K, Baeumner AJ
candidates.abstract: Liposome-based bioassays take advantage of liposomes' immense signaling power and easy surface modification. Photometric, electrochemical, and fluorescent detection methods dominate their application in bioassays. Here, it is studied how covalent modification of the liposome surface with proteins affects the functionality of entrapped enzymes. Horseradish peroxidase (HRP) was selected as a model for entrapment while streptavidin served as a model surface ligand. Several coupling reagents negatively affected the functionality of entrapped HRP. In the case of EDC-sNHS chemistry, membrane-permeable reagents inactivated HRP. Similarly, when applying copper-free click chemistry, in particular strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC), azide-functionalized lipids caused enzyme inactivation probably through coordination with the prosthetic heme iron of HRP. In contrast, the inverse approach employing DBCO-functionalized lipids fully preserved HRP activity. Under optimized conditions with coupling times of only 24 h at room temperature, streptavidin coupling efficiencies reached standard levels. Entrapped HRP was stabilized with 310 mM trehalose and 2 mg/mL HSA enabling storage for up to 6 months after streptavidin modification. HRP-loaded liposomes were evaluated by adapting an assay for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibodies in serum. Therefore, the liposome surface was modified with the receptor binding domain (RBD) of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. The RBD-modified liposomes with simple photometric detection demonstrated a similar sensitivity as fluorescent sulforhodamine B (SRB) liposomes, with a strong correlation of both methods (Pearson's r = 0.987). HRP liposomes are hence a reliable platform for visual or photometric bioassays providing similar limits of detection as fluorescent approaches making them ideal for routine lab and point-of-care applications.

candidates.title: Trastuzumab deruxtecan kills skin and uveal melanoma in vivo by HER2-independent payload release
candidates.authors: Nilsson, L. M., Tanaydin, E. S., Stenqvist, S., et al.
candidates.abstract: Background: HER2-directed CAR-T cells can eradicate melanoma despite low HER2 expression. We therefore asked whether melanoma would also respond to trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), an antibody-drug conjugate targeting HER2. Patients and methods: T-DXd was evaluated in several patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models and as a compassionate use in one patient with metastatic uveal melanoma. We compared T-DXd with another ADC, trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1), and examined ADC sensitivity and trastuzumab uptake in vitro, and expression of HER2 and cathepsin L (CTSL) in xenografts. Results: T-DXd inhibited all subcutaneous PDXs, while liver models were less sensitive. T-DM1 had limited activity. Unexpectedly, parental and ERBB2-knockout melanoma xenografts showed similar initial responses to T-DXd, although knockout tumors regrew earlier. Tumor-derived CTSL was detected outside melanoma cells in the xenografts. Melanoma cells were largely resistant to both ADCs in vitro and showed little trastuzumab uptake compared to HER2-amplified breast cancer cells. Conclusions: T-DXd has a substantial HER2-independent component of activity in the tested melanoma xenografts. Presence of extracellular CTSL, an enzyme known to cleave T-Dxd, provide a possibility that linker cleavage and payload release can occur outside of the tumor cells.

candidates.title: Diacylglycerol Kinases Balance DAG Signaling to Control B Cell Maturation, Germinal Center Homeostasis, and Humoral Immunity
candidates.authors: Xie, J., Zhang, S., Lee, W., et al.
candidates.abstract: Diacylglycerol (DAG) is a critical second messenger downstream of the B-cell receptor (BCR), but how DAG signaling is regulated during B-cell development and humoral responses remains incompletely understood. Here, complementary gain- and loss-of-function approaches revealed stage-specific requirements for diacylglycerol kinase (DGK)-regulated signaling in B cells. Expression of the gain-of-function DGK{zeta} mutant DGK{zeta}{Delta}NLS had limited effects on early BM B-cell development but progressively impaired transitional and mature B-cell populations. DGK{zeta}{Delta}NLS attenuated BCR-induced ERK1/2 and mTOR signaling, activation, and proliferation and, when expressed in AID-expressing B cells, reduced GC B-cell survival and T-dependent IgG responses without detectably impairing GC B-cell proliferation in vivo. Conversely, combined DGK/{zeta} deficiency resulted in marked spontaneous GC B-cell expansion associated with enhanced ERK1/2, Akt, and S6 signaling and increased glucose uptake. Despite this steady-state GC expansion, DGK/{zeta}-deficient mice developed spontaneous autoreactivity and mounted impaired antigen-specific antibody responses. Thus, B-cell developmental stages exhibit differential sensitivity to altered DGK activity, and opposing perturbations of DGK-regulated signaling produce reciprocal effects on GC B-cell accumulation while both compromise productive humoral immunity. These findings identify DGKs as critical regulators that tune lipid signaling for B-cell maturation, GC homeostasis, and effective antibody responses.

candidates.title: A Tandem Fluorescent Rh1::eGFP mCherry Reporter Reveals Rhodopsin 1 Trafficking and Turnover In Vivo in Drosophila Photoreceptors
candidates.authors: Gheflati, H., Steiner, C., Feizy, N.
candidates.abstract: Rhodopsin 1 (Rh1), the major visual pigment of Drosophila photoreceptors, requires a vitamin A-derived chromophore for proper folding, maturation and transport to the rhabdomere. While the endocytic trafficking of mature, light-activated Rh1 to endolysosomal compartments is well characterized, the fate of immature Rh1 during defective ER maturation remains unclear. Here, we developed a Rh1::eGFP-mCherry tandem reporter to monitor Rh1 localization and compartment acidification in vivo. Exploiting the acid stability of mCherry, this reporter enables visualization of Rh1 after delivery to acidic environments and complements conventional antibody-based approaches. Under physiological conditions, pH-dependent quenching of eGFP fluorescence distinguished rhabdomeric Rh1 from Rh1 in acidic endolysosomal compartments. In vitamin A-deficient flies, immature apo-Rh1 accumulated within Calnexin-positive ER membranes, where we identified discrete acidified subdomains characterized by loss of eGFP fluorescence while mCherry fluorescence persisted. These structures remained continuous with the ER but were distinct from conventional endolysosomal compartments, revealing previously unrecognized acidified ER domains associated with immature Rh1. Together, our findings identify acidified ER subdomains as a previously unrecognized stage in Rh1 quality control and establish Rh1::eGFP-mCherry as a robust in vivo reporter for investigating rhodopsin trafficking, maturation and turnover under physiological and disease-relevant conditions.

candidates.title: Worldwide diversity and geographic structure of killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptor (KIR) gene content
candidates.authors: Obeso Fernandez, A.
candidates.abstract: Introduction: Killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptor (KIR) gene content shapes natural killer-cell responses and varies substantially among populations. We examined whether worldwide KIR diversity reflects regional structure, isolation by distance, serial founder effects, or latitudinal gradients. Data and methods: Carrier frequencies for 11 variable KIR genes were obtained from the Allele Frequency Net Database. The primary analysis included 189 locally sampled, non-diaspora, non-mixed populations from 70 countries, comprising 25,469 individuals; 161 populations had complete 11-gene profiles. Diversity indices, ordination, clustering, permutation-based variance decomposition, Mantel tests, and regression models were used to characterize geographic structure. Serial founder effects were evaluated using four distance measures from East Africa, both globally and within the Old World. Models of latitude incorporated spatial autocorrelation. Prespecified sensitivity analyses evaluated alternative population sets, gene panels, geographic classifications, weighting schemes, and multivariate outlier exclusion. Results: Geographic region explained 53.5% of variation in KIR profiles, substantially exceeding the permutation-null expectation of 6.9%, although multivariate dispersion differed among regions. Twenty-five of 28 pairwise regional comparisons remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction. Isolation by distance was modest (Mantel r=0.3003) and weakened after controlling for region (r=0.1557). KIR diversity did not decline with distance from East Africa globally but decreased strongly within the Old World (expected heterozygosity {beta}=-0.0066 and standardized gene content {beta}=-0.0789). B-content decreased nominally with absolute latitude, but latitude was collinear with region and the association survived neither spatial modelling nor sensitivity analyses. Regional differentiation remained robust across analytical specifications, whereas the Old World decline was carried by gene content once standard errors were clustered by country. Conclusion: Worldwide KIR gene-content variation shows pronounced regional differentiation, modest isolation by distance, and no independent latitudinal gradient. Diversity declines with distance from East Africa across the Old World, supporting serial founder effects, but not once the Americas and Oceania are included.

candidates.title: Full stack academic publishing in seizures with artificial intelligence: a cautionary tale
candidates.authors: Kerr, W. T., Pellinen, J., McFarlane, K. N., et al.
candidates.abstract:
SignificanceThere is potential for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to perform "full stack" academic publishing, including comprehensive manuscript fabrication, "peer"-review, and editorial decision making. This study evaluated the benefits and cautions in using AI for full stack academic publishing in clinical research about seizures.

MethodsThree epileptologists each selected 1 published manuscript in Epilepsia and produced an AI-fabricated manuscript about seizures. AI tools were then used to perform "peer"-review and make editorial decisions with minimal human supervision. The rates of identifying AI-fabricated manuscripts and editorial decisions among the epileptologists was analyzed, and epileptologists observations on how AI differed from typical human "peer"-review and editorial decisions was collected.

ResultsFour of 6 (67%) pairs of AI-fabricated and human-generated manuscripts were correctly identified. Only 1 AI-fabricated manuscript was editorially rejected, whereas another had a subtle indicator of fabrication. When compared to human content, AI generated content was comprehensive, detailed, and based on the highest standard of academic publication. However, generated content was more verbose, used more structured responses, and more critical feedback.

ConclusionsThese results demonstrate that the quality of AI-fabricated manuscripts about clinical research in seizures was sufficiently high that the current methods of peer and editorial review could not easily distinguish fabricated content compared to human-written content. Moreover, AI review and editorial decisions were high quality and appeared reasonable in many cases. AI tools have matured to the point that there should be thoughtful policies that permit AI assistance but prohibit insufficiently supervised autonomous scientific submissions, reviews, and editorial decisions.

Highlights- The maturity of AI tools to assist in manuscript generation, peer-review, and editorial decisions comes with cautions.
- Only 1 of 3 artificial intelligence (AI) fabricated manuscripts about seizures were reliably identified and rejected.
- This study describes characteristics of AI-generated peer-review and editorial comments that had insufficient human oversight.

candidates.title: Emerging novel therapies for the treatment of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
candidates.authors: Al-Samkari H
candidates.abstract: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia is the second most common heritable bleeding disorder worldwide, with a prevalence more than twice that of haemophilia, and is the most morbid inherited bleeding disorder of women. As an autosomal dominant vasculopathy due to dysregulated angiogenic signalling, patients with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia develop telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations which cause numerous complications. These complications include moderate-to-severe chronic epistaxis, gastrointestinal bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, and requirement for intravenous iron or red cell transfusion. Additionally, incidence of intracranial haemorrhage is high and morbid non-bleeding complications, such as venous thromboembolism, stroke, and liver disease, are common. Despite this serious disease burden, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia remains without licensed therapies worldwide. However, many novel, investigational agents targeting vascular and haemostatic systems are now rapidly undergoing formal development specifically in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. These agents include the selective AKT1/AKT2 inhibitor engasertib, AKT1-selective inhibitors ATV-1601 and TER-4480, plasminogen siRNA agent ALN-6400, activin receptor-like kinase 1-bone morphogenetic protein receptor type II (ALK1-BMPRII) bispecific clustering antibody DIAG723, and apelin receptor antagonist antibody TX2100. This comprehensive Review provides essential background information and illustrations summarising relevant hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia pathophysiology, followed by focused, detailed discussions of each of the novel agents in development, including the mechanisms, therapeutic rationale, clinical trial programmes, and potential therapeutic effects.

candidates.title: CD19 CAR Engineered T Regulatory Cells Promote Durable Immune Tolerance in Experimental Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
candidates.authors: Drow, T., Doglio, M., Grimm, A., et al.
candidates.abstract: While the immune reset induced by CD19 CAR T therapies has shown striking promise in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the nature and duration of benefit mediated by B cell depletion remains unclear. Loss of tolerance in SLE is driven by extrafollicular and germinal center interactions between dendritic cells and self-reactive T and B cells. We hypothesized that CD19 CAR-engineered regulatory T cells (CAR19 EngTreg), capable of suppressing multiple autoimmune effector cell types, might promote long-term tolerance without producing high-levels of inflammatory mediators. To generate CAR19 EngTreg, we combined CD19 CAR delivery with homology directed repair at the FOXP3 locus to drive constitutive, stable FOXP3 expression in CD4 T cells. CAR19 EngTreg expressed canonical Treg markers; exhibited minimal inflammatory cytokine production; and blocked human B cell differentiation into antibody secreting plasma cells. In humanized mouse models, transfer of CAR19 EngTreg led to a reduction in B cell numbers with low inflammatory cytokine production relative to CD19 CAR Teff, and reduced tissue inflammation. In a short-term, in vivo imiquimod-induced inflammatory model, murine CAR19 EngTreg reduced skin pathology, spleen size, and inflammatory cytokines. Finally, in two distinct mouse models of lupus, CAR19 EngTreg persisted for >4 months leading to reduced autoimmune T and B effector populations, sustained reduction in multiple autoantibodies and improved renal function and histopathology. Thus, CAR19 EngTreg may offer a promising and durable therapeutic avenue for B cell-mediated autoimmune disorders capable of long-term regulation of both autoreactive B and T cells.

candidates.title: NGS-Guided Discovery of Cross-Reactive TfR1 VHH Antibodies with Distinct Brain Localization Profiles.
candidates.authors: Jatnika MF, Nagashima A, Miyahara W, et al.
candidates.abstract: Antibody delivery across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) remains challenging. We combined phage display with next-generation sequencing (NGS)-guided clone sequence-diverse selection to identify transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1)-binding VHH antibodies. Following alpacas immunization with human and rat TfR1, representative clones from distinct phylogenetic groups were screened for human/mouse cross-reactivity. Three clones (A1, Y11, and Z1) were reformatted as human Fc-mutant fusion proteins and characterized by ELISA, flow cytometry, and fluorescence imaging. All three clones recognized human and mouse TfR1, with ELISA EC₅₀ >100 nM. After intravenous administration in mice, clone Y11 showed sustained brain-associated fluorescence up to 48 h, whereas A1 showed an initially high signal that progressively declined. Fluorescent microscopy revealed preferential localization of Y11 to NeuN-positive neuronal regions, whereas A1 to lectin-positive vascular structures, indicating distinct brain localization profiles among the isolated clones. These findings identify cross-reactive TfR1-targeting VHHs with distinct brain-localization profiles and potential utility as platforms for compartment-selective CNS drug delivery.

candidates.title: Time-Evolving Immunomodulatory Activity in Green-Fixed Devitalized Cellular Materials
candidates.authors: Correia, M., Atila, D., Mota-Silva, E., et al.
candidates.abstract: By decoupling biological function from cellular viability, fixed abiotic cellular materials have emerged as a promising platform for next-generation immunotherapies, preserving essential immunomodulatory activities while enabling unprecedented control over manufacturing, storage, and standardization. Nevertheless, the coupled effects of fabrication history and post-fabrication environmental cues on their biological functionality remain elusive. Here, we show that both preparation route and storage time critically affect the bioactivity of mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-derived microtissues. By exploring different devitalization agents, we demonstrate that an ethanol-based strategy provides a green fixation option with comparable preservation of volumetric and fixed cell architecture, as well as immunomodulatory function. Processing protocols did not merely substitute conventional fixation but tailored specific immune-related bioactivity. An unexpected processing protocol and time-dependent enhancement of immunomodulatory performance was observed, with ethanol-fixed microtissues maintaining a stable baseline bioactive profile while increasing functional potency over 8 weeks of storage. We establish a framework for the design of immunomodulatory abiotic cell-derived materials with potential for the treatment of immune-mediated diseases and regenerative therapies, and we hope that the principles uncovered here may contribute to a broader understanding of how devitalized tissues can be engineered, preserved, and functionally tuned, whether lab-made or derived from natural biological systems.

candidates.title: Polysaccharide-based drug conjugates and related delivery systems for Alzheimer's disease: from molecular design to translational challenges.
candidates.authors: Nguyen NH, Le HT, Thi Nguyen NT, et al.
candidates.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) presents distinct extracellular, intracellular and vascular delivery targets, yet brain exposure of candidate therapeutics remains difficult to establish. This narrative review compares hyaluronic acid, chitosan, cyclodextrin, dextran, alginate and pectin systems by construct architecture, route, blood-brain barrier (BBB) evidence, cargo release and biological response. The literature includes covalent drug conjugates, loaded or coated carriers, host-guest complexes and intrinsically active polymers; evidence from one category cannot validate another. Clinical programs involving intravenous hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin and a transferrin-receptor antibody shuttle provide context, but do not establish BBB transport for the conjugates reviewed. We examine how polymer size and degradation influence immune safety, particularly chitosan-associated NLRP3 activation and context-dependent responses to hyaluronic acid fragments. We distinguish endothelial or whole-brain signal from parenchymal active-drug exposure, and discuss payload-specific endosomal escape. Advancement requires a defined construct, quantitative target-site exposure, target engagement, comparison with free drug and a matched carrier, and route-appropriate safety data.

candidates.title: Novel EG95-based mRNA vaccines induce long-term protective immunity against echinococcosis.
candidates.authors: Chen WG, Li L, Dai GD, et al.
candidates.abstract: Cystic echinococcosis (CE), a neglected zoonotic disease caused by Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato, remains a significant public health and veterinary concern worldwide. Despite efforts to develop recombinant protein-based vaccines against EG95, a key protective antigen, existing platforms suffer from limited immunogenicity, short-lived immunity, and complex production processes. Here, we designed and evaluated three novel mRNA-LNP vaccines, including EG95 mRNA-LNP vaccine, IL-4-EG95 mRNA-LNP vaccine encoding EG95 fused with IL-4 via a flexible linker to enhance immune stimulation, and EG95-EC95 mRNA-LNP vaccine that multivalent formulation incorporating EC95 antigens from Echinococcus canadensis. The vaccine candidates were efficiently encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles and demonstrated robust target expression in vitro and in vivo. Immunization induced significantly stronger, more durable humoral and cellular immune responses compared to a commercial EG95 subunit vaccine both in mice and lambs. Notably, high levels of specific antibodies persisted for over 12 months post-vaccination. Parasites infection challenge experiments confirmed that these three mRNA-LNP vaccines, especially the IL-4-EG95 vaccine conferred superior protection, inhibited protoscolex survival and cyst growth. These results highlight the advantages of mRNA-based vaccines in safety, scalability, and flexibility over conventional approaches, offering a promising strategy for controlling E. granulosus sensu lato transmission and reducing the zoonotic burden of CE.

candidates.title: NECTIN4 defines a subtype-dependent tumor state coupling enfortumab vedotin targetability to antitumor immunity in bladder cancer
candidates.authors: Nishimura, K., Maenosono, R., Owari, T., et al.
candidates.abstract: NECTIN4 is the target of enfortumab vedotin (EV), but its biological role in bladder cancer (BC) and its relationship to EV plus PD-1 blockade remain unclear. Integrating clinical multi-omics, spatial and single-cell immune profiling, and experimental models, we identify NECTIN4 as a subtype-dependent determinant of tumor state and antitumor immunity. In basal BC cells, NECTIN4 suppressed inflammatory and mesenchymal programs. Consistently, NECTIN4-high basal/squamous muscle-invasive BCs showed favorable survival, higher checkpoint inhibitor response rates, and a coordinated CD8+ T cell-inflamed microenvironment with no comparable associations in luminal papillary tumors. In orthotopic models, murine Nectin4 promoted CD8+ T cell-dependent tumor control, whereas human NECTIN4 conferred EV sensitivity. EV also attenuated NECTIN4-dependent TIGIT binding. Conversely, NECTIN4-low models were preferentially sensitive to HDAC inhibition. NECTIN4 therefore couples antibody-drug conjugate targetability to a subtype-specific tumor-immune state permissive for checkpoint blockade, whereas the NECTIN4-low state defines a distinct inflammatory-mesenchymal state with an alternative therapeutic vulnerability.

candidates.title: HPV binding antibodies are associated with protection: a meta-analysis
candidates.authors: Berry, M. T., Palmer, M. R., Khan, S. R., et al.
candidates.abstract:
BackgroundHuman papillomavirus (HPV) is the major cause of cervical cancer globally. Current vaccines have shown high efficacy at preventing HPV infection and other surrogate disease endpoints in randomised controlled trials (RCT). However, uptake is limited by accessibility and cost. Rapid clinical evaluation is critical for shortening time-to-market and encouraging the development and deployment of affordable vaccines. We aim to establish a validated correlate of protection that will support vaccine developers and decision makers with vaccine development, approval, dose schedules and deployment decisions.

MethodsWe utilised three existing Cochrane Systematic Reviews of RCTs of HPV vaccines and extended these to 1st January 2026. We identified and extracted data from trials where both efficacy and immunogenicity (HPV-specific antibodies) were reported. For HPV types where vaccine efficacy was reported but not immunogenicity (Types 31/33/45/52/58) we sourced antibody binding concentrations from separate immunogenicity studies. We linked antibody binding concentrations from each RCT to the corresponding vaccine efficacy data, matching by study, vaccine arm, number of doses, and HPV type. We use a Bayesian framework in a model-based meta-analysis to examine the association between antibody binding concentrations and vaccine efficacy.

FindingsCombining data on both vaccine-targeted and non-targeted HPV types, we find an association between type-specific antibody binding concentrations and vaccine efficacy against the three HPV outcomes tested: incident infection, persistent infection and grade 2 or 3 cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN2+) (p < 0.0005, for all outcomes). We also compared this association with data from studies of natural infection, which had shown an association between antibody binding concentrations and risk of infection. This demonstrated that the association between vaccine-induced antibodies and vaccine efficacy was well aligned with the existing HPV literature on correlates of risk from natural exposure. Finally, we find evidence that the antibody concentrations associated with 50% (of the maximal) vaccine efficacy differ by type (p < 0.0005, for example 16 sIU/ml for HPV58, but < 0.5 IU/ml for HPV 16/18).

InterpretationsHPV type-specific antibody binding concentrations are associated with protection against HPV related clinical outcomes, across different HPV types and vaccines, and after natural infection. The consistent observation that antibody binding concentrations correlate with protection provides support for the use of antibody binding for immunobridging, for example in non-inferiority studies when assessing similar vaccines.

FundingThis work is supported by National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia and the University of New South Wales.

candidates.title: Fluorescence-based sorting of extracellular vesicles enables detection and omics
candidates.authors: Clos-Sansalvador, M., Monguio-Tortajada, M., Garcia, S. G., et al.
candidates.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are nanosized, lipid bilayer-enclosed particles that mediate intercellular communication and hold considerable promise as biomarkers and therapeutic agents. However, their functional heterogeneity remains incompletely understood, largely due to the absence of reliable methods for isolating specific EV subpopulations. Here, we established a Nanoscale Flow sorting (NanoFACS) workflow and evaluated its potential for EV detection, sorting, and molecular characterization. We assessed critical parameters, including fluorescent staining and labeling approaches, background signal discrimination, dilution and flow-rate effects, and scatter triggering. We achieved high-purity sorting of CFSE-stained and antibody-labeled EVs, preserving vesicle integrity and sufficient RNA yields for small RNA sequencing of sorted populations. We identified EV subtype-specific small RNAs despite partial cargo overlap in single-marker sorted populations. Our results establish a reproducible antibody-based NanoFACS workflow that defines key operational parameters for reliable EV detection and sorting, with potential adaptability across conventional and spectral flow cytometry platforms. By reducing background and non-EV-associated events, the workflow enables the isolation of phenotypically defined EV subpopulations suitable for downstream molecular analysis, providing a practical approach to investigate EV heterogeneity.

candidates.title: A multivalent mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine containing eight hemagglutinin antigens elicited broad neutralizing antibody responses and protected against influenza A virus challenge in swine.
candidates.authors: Ciacci Zanella G, Vincent ML, Flores L, et al.
candidates.abstract: The diversity within H1 and H3 subtype influenza A viruses (IAVs) in swine prevents effective vaccine control approaches with inactivated whole-virus vaccines. We addressed the challenge of controlling co-circulating hemagglutinin (HA) clades of swine IAV with the development of a multivalent messenger RNA (mRNA)-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing eight HA proteins to maximize genetic coverage. We applied a computational approach to select eight HA genes that represented 95% of the observed IAVs detected in the United States between 2022 and 2025. Piglets were vaccinated and boosted intramuscularly with either individual HA mRNA-LNP or an 8-HA multivalent mRNA-LNP. Serum was collected to evaluate systemic antibody levels. Twenty-one days post-boost, pigs were challenged with a field-relevant H1 1A.3.3.3-c3 IAV strain. The 8-HA multivalent mRNA-LNP vaccine induced neutralizing antibodies against all eight antigens, and vaccinees were protected against lung lesions, with lesion scores similar to non-challenged animals. Homologous monovalent vaccination significantly reduced IAV detection in nasal secretions and in the lungs. Heterologous monovalent vaccination was not cross-protective but did not induce vaccine-associated enhanced respiratory disease. We provide evidence that monovalent and multivalent mRNA-LNP influenza vaccines elicited neutralizing antibody responses in pigs and protected against viral challenge. The versatility and capacity for rapidly updating the mRNA-LNP vaccine platform make it an appealing tool to improve animal health and minimize the circulation and diversity of IAV in swine.IMPORTANCEInfluenza A virus (IAV) is an important respiratory pathogen in swine, and zoonotic transmission of swine strains to humans remains a public health risk. Control strategies against IAV in swine herds rely heavily on biosecurity measures and vaccination. However, the antigenic diversity of IAV circulating in swine challenges current vaccination programs, and there is a need for broadly protective vaccines or platforms that can rapidly update components to reflect circulating diversity. mRNA-LNP vaccines have emerged as promising vaccine platforms, offering simultaneous delivery of multiple antigens, rapid development, scalable manufacturing, and potent immunogenicity. In this study, we assessed the immunogenicity and protective capacity of monovalent and multivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines encoding eight representative IAV hemagglutinin (HA) antigens. To our knowledge, this is the first study to objectively select multiple representative endemic swine IAV strains by quantifying genetic diversity within the phylogeny and to apply this selection to rationally design and evaluate a multivalent HA mRNA-based influenza vaccine in the swine model.

candidates.title: The MRTFs are required for thymocyte trafficking and Treg-mediated immune tolerance
candidates.authors: Costello, P., Maurice, D., Benito-Jardon, M., et al.
candidates.abstract: The MRTFs (myocardin-related transcription factors) are essential for effective cytoskeletal function during differentiation and development. To investigate the role played by the MRTFs in T cell development and function we inactivated Mrtfb in Mrtfa-null mice at the DN2 stage (MrtfabKOT animals). Positive selection, and development of MrtfabKOT regulatory (Treg), {gamma}{delta}, and NK T cells proceeded normally. Thymic egress was impaired, however, with mature T cells accumulating at the cortico-medullary junction, and in vitro MrtfabKOT thymocytes exhibited impaired cytoskeletal responses to S1P and migratory cytokines. MrtfabKOT mice were lymphopenic, with defective homeostatic proliferation and T cell homing to peripheral lymphoid organs. Although thymocyte negative selection was unaffected, MrtfabKOT animals develop autoimmune phenotypes in lacrimal gland and intestinal mucosa. Using the experimental colitis model, we show that these phenotypes reflect functional deficits in MrtfabKOT Treg cells. Our findings show that MRTF-SRF signalling plays an unanticipated role in thymocyte egress and immune tolerance, and reveal a role of the MRTFs in Treg function.

candidates.title: Protein Nanocages as Tunable Stoichiometric Benchmarks for Quantitative SMLM.
candidates.authors: Colosi PL, Hugelier S, Lakadamyali M
candidates.abstract: Quantitative interpretation of single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) data remains limited by fluorophore blinking, incomplete or variable labeling, and the lack of calibration standards that are tunable, synthetic, and compatible with cellular imaging. Here, we evaluate self-assembling protein nanocages as stoichiometric benchmarks for copy-number calibration in STORM imaging. We generated mammalian expression constructs encoding nanocages containing 60- or 120-copies of different GFP variants and repositioned the fluorescent protein to the N-terminus to improve accessibility for anti-GFP nanobody labeling. Among the variants tested, mCitrine-tagged nanocages showed the most consistent expression and labeling with commercially available AF647-conjugated anti-GFP nanobodies. Using an analysis pipeline that matched widefield-detected nanocages to STORM-localized clusters, we found that mCitrine 120-mer nanocages produced localization distribution in which the mean of the distribution was shifted by approximately two-fold compared to the 60-mer. These results suggest that optimized protein nanocages can serve as useful calibration standards for STORM in the moderate to high copy-number range. More broadly, this approach provides a flexible framework that could be extended to additional nanocage stoichiometries, labeling strategies, and SMLM modalities.

candidates.title: Multivalent protein nanocages improve the safety profile of cluster of differentiation 47 checkpoint blockade.
candidates.authors: Ahn W, Kim S, Lee Y, et al.
candidates.abstract: Protein-based nanocages are emerging as promising platforms for next-generation medicine because of their programmable architecture, biocompatibility, and capacity for functional integration. In the field of immunotherapy, these properties offer a structural basis for overcoming key limitations of conventional antibody-based therapeutics, where potent checkpoint blockade activity is often accompanied by systemic toxicity. Here, we demonstrate that a ferritin-signal regulatory protein alpha (SIRPα) protein nanocage maintains the therapeutic function of cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47)-SIRPα blockade while reducing the hematologic liabilities associated with CD47-targeting monoclonal antibodies. Although the CD47-SIRPα axis is a compelling innate immune checkpoint target broadly implicated in tumor immune evasion, anti-CD47 antibodies have been limited by the widespread expression of CD47 on both tumor cells and normal erythrocytes, which can result in dose-limiting hematologic toxicity. By displaying multivalent SIRPα domains on a self-assembling ferritin scaffold, ferritin-SIRPα achieves CD47 engagement through a structurally distinct, Fc-independent nanocage architecture. In direct comparison with anti-CD47 antibody, ferritin-SIRPα showed no hemagglutination at equivalent or higher doses, preserved near-complete viability across diverse immune and hematopoietic cell types, and avoided the reduction in RBC counts observed with anti-CD47 antibody treatment in vivo. Ferritin-SIRPα induced macrophage-mediated tumor cell phagocytosis under single-agent conditions, with further enhancement observed upon combination with EGFR antibody-mediated opsonization, indicating that its innate immune engagement remains functionally intact. These findings demonstrate that multivalent protein nanocage architecture can decouple antitumor immune activity from erythrocyte-associated toxicity. Broadly, this study highlights the potential of protein nanocages as a versatile therapeutic platform for preserving functional efficacy while mitigating off-target adverse effects, offering a structural strategy that may help improve the therapeutic window of next-generation immunotherapies.

candidates.title: Single-molecule force spectroscopy of ligand-receptor mechanics at extracellular vesicle biointerfaces.
candidates.authors: Tani S, Jacobson R, Ha S, et al.
candidates.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are nanoscale membrane-bound particles that present surface receptors for affinity capture, sensing, and targeted biointerface design. Although EV surface-marker expression is widely used to guide ligand selection, the molecular-scale rupture mechanics and force-dependent dissociation behavior of EV receptor-ligand interactions remain poorly understood. Here, atomic force microscopy-based single-molecule force spectroscopy and dynamic force spectroscopy are used to quantify ligand-accessible recognition, rupture-force distributions, and apparent Bell-Evans parameters for three pancreatic cancer-associated EV surface targets: integrins (ITG), epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM), and glypican-1 (GPC1). EVs derived from PANC-1 and hTERT-HPNE cells were compared as a model system. PANC-1 EVs exhibited higher particle concentrations and stronger ITG and GPC1 expression than HPNE EVs. AFM recognition maps showed markedly higher apparent ITG recognition and moderately higher GPC1 recognition on PANC-1 EVs, whereas EpCAM recognition was similar between the two EV preparations. Fixed-speed rupture-force distributions and loading-rate-dependent analysis revealed interaction-dependent differences in apparent rupture behavior. Across both EV preparations, EpCAM-antibody interactions tended to show higher apparent force-free off-rates than ITG-cRGD and GPC1-antibody interactions, while ITG and GPC1 were less clearly separated. Together with recognition mapping, these results demonstrate that ligand-accessible recognition and force-dependent rupture behavior provide complementary information about EV surface interactions.

candidates.title: Redefining breast cancer treatment by precision oncology: the clinical impact of sacituzumab govitecan.
candidates.authors: Di Lauro V, Sacco PC, Palma V, et al.
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Trophoblast cell-surface antigen-2 (Trop-2) is overexpressed in most breast cancers, including about 90% of triple-negative breast cancers (TNBC) and more than half of hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative (HR+/HER2-) tumors, with limited expression in normal tissues, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Sacituzumab govitecan (SG), the first Trop-2-directed antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) delivers the topoisomerase I inhibitor SN-38 to cancer cells and has changed the treatment of metastatic breast cancer (mBC). AREAS COVERED: This review synthesizes data from chemical characterization, pharmacokinetic studies, and the clinical evidence from phases I-III in metastatic TNBC and HR+/HER2- mBC (IMMU-132-01, ASCENT, ASCENT-03, ASCENT-04, ASCENT-07, TROPiCS-02) and in early-stage disease. A literature search from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and ClinicalTrials.gov, complemented by the proceedings of the ASCO, ESMO, and SABCS meetings, was performed up to September 2026 using the terms 'sacituzumab govitecan,' 'Trop-2,' 'antibody-drug conjugates,' and 'breast cancer'. EXPERT OPINION: The high drug-to-antibody ratio, membrane-permeable payload and bystander effect of SG explain both its efficacy and its hematological and gastrointestinal toxicity. Its place among the growing family of Trop-2-directed and topoisomerase I payload ADCs will depend on rational sequencing, biomarkers of resistance, and combination with immunotherapy and poly-ADP-ribose polymerase inhibitors.

candidates.title: Preservation of intracellular protein-protein interactions in archived cytological specimens: Optimization of preanalytical variables for in situ proximity ligation assay
candidates.authors: Dahlstrom, C. M., Hirsch, J. M., Lof, L.
candidates.abstract: Context: Cytological specimens allow minimally invasive, repeated sampling for diagnosis and molecular testing. However, cytology biobanking protocols have primarily been optimized for morphology, and the effects of preanalytical handling and storage on intracellular proteins remain unclear. Objective: To assess how fixation, staining, storage temperature, and duration affect intracellular protein preservation in cytological specimens and to identify conditions suitable for in situ proximity ligation assay (isPLA). Design: Human cancer cell lines were processed under different preanalytical conditions. Intracellular proteins and protein protein interactions were assessed by isPLA, fluorescence microscopy, and quantitative image analysis. Slides were stored at room temperature or minus 20 Celsius, with or without MayGrunwaldGiemsa (MGG) staining. Results: Storage temperature had the greatest effect on protein signal. Unstained slides stored at minus 20 Celsius retained strong signals for up to 24 months, whereas room temperature storage reduced detectable protein interactions by approximately 95%. MGG staining further reduced signal intensity during prolonged storage. Nevertheless, stained slides remained suitable for isPLA when staining, microscopic evaluation, destaining, and antibody labeling were completed on the same day. Prolonged room temperature storage of stained slides caused loss of antigenicity, increased autofluorescence, and false negative findings. Conclusions: Low temperature storage and standardized preanalytical handling preserve intracellular protein signals in cytological specimens. These conditions support reliable single cell protein profiling of archived samples and their use in biomarker research and translational pathology.

candidates.title: Preclinical Characterization of ADCT-241, an Exatecan-Based Antibody-Drug Conjugate Against PSMA for the Treatment of Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer.
candidates.authors: Jabeen A, Leatherdale B, Martin R, et al.
candidates.abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a type II transmembrane glycoprotein with elevated expression in primary and metastatic prostate cancer (PCa) compared with normal prostate tissues; with low levels in renal proximal tubules, small intestine, and the brain. PSMA is a clinically validated target and is associated with progression and aggressiveness of disease. ADCT-241 is a novel antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) composed of the fully human monoclonal antibody (mAb) 2A10, directed against PSMA, to which the exatecan-containing PL2202 payload was stochastically conjugated with a drug-to-antibody ratio of 4. 2A10 was selected over J591, as it showed good binding affinity, a better half-life, and superior internalization properties and antitumor activity compared with a J591-based ADC. ADCT-241 showed specific, potent killing of PCa cell lines in vitro and antitumor efficacy in vivo in PCa cell line and patient-derived xenografts. ADCT-241 showed target-dependent internalization, topoisomerase 1 (TOP1) inhibition, cell cycle arrest at G2/M phase followed by apoptosis-induced cell death, and in vitro bystander activity. In rats and cynomolgus monkeys, ADCT-241 was well tolerated at dose levels ≤150 and 75 mg/kg, respectively, following dosing on day 1 and 22. Circulating serum total antibody, total ADC, and free exatecan concentrations showed good in vivo stability and a half-life of 8 to 10 days in cynomolgus monkeys. ADCT-241 demonstrated potent, specific in vitro and in vivo antitumor activity and it was stable and well tolerated in rats and cynomolgus monkeys, warranting progression of ADCT-241 into clinical trials in patients with metastatic castration-resistant PCa.

candidates.title: Lysostaphin bioengineered cascade nanoreactor for bacterial eradication and inflammatory remodeling in MRSA pneumonia.
candidates.authors: Pan X, Liu F, Kang R, et al.
candidates.abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) pneumonia is a life-threatening infectious disease, yet current antibiotic-centered therapies remain insufficient to achieve satisfactory therapeutic outcomes. Herein, a lysostaphin-bioengineered cascade nanoreactor, LO-PDA/Zn@CA, is developed for the integrated treatment of MRSA pneumonia. This system consists of cinnamaldehyde (CA)-loaded, Zn2+-chelated polydopamine nanoparticles coated with lysostaphin-engineered bacterial outer membrane vesicles. Upon reaching MRSA-infected lung lesions, CA disrupts the biofilm matrix and compromises bacterial membranes, thereby weakening extracellular protective barriers. Zn2+ subsequently activates surface-displayed lysostaphin to specifically hydrolyze pentaglycine cross-bridges within the MRSA peptidoglycan cell wall, further breaching bacterial integrity and promoting intrabacterial penetration of CA and Zn2+. The released Zn2+ induces lethal DNA damage-associated responses, collectively amplifying bactericidal efficacy through a stepwise antibacterial cascade. In parallel, the PDA/Zn nanocore scavenges excessive reactive oxygen species, suppresses glycolytic reprogramming, and downregulates H3K27ac-dependent transcription of pro-inflammatory genes, thereby attenuating macrophage M1 polarization and mitigating pulmonary inflammatory injury. In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrate that LO-PDA/Zn@CA effectively eliminates planktonic MRSA, disrupts established biofilms, and alleviates MRSA-induced pulmonary inflammation with favorable biosafety. By integrating pathogen-specific bacterial eradication with inflammation resolution in a cascade manner, this work provides a versatile nanotherapeutic strategy for the treatment of drug-resistant MRSA pneumonia.

candidates.title: Differential Effects of Distinct Type I Interferons and IFN Inducers on Fc Receptor landscape and myeloid cell function
candidates.authors: Bru, R., Paris, O., Bossis, G., et al.
candidates.abstract: Antiviral monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) rely on Fc-mediated effector functions, which depend on interactions with Fc receptors (FcRs) expressed on immune cells such as monocytes and dendritic cells (DCs). While combinations of antiviral mAbs with type I interferons (IFN-I) or IFN inducers are being explored to enhance therapeutic efficacy, the impact of these immunomodulators on FcR expression remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of IFN-2, IFN-{beta}, and the IFN-inducer TAK-981 (a SUMOylation inhibitor) on FcR modulation and functional activation in human monocyte subsets and monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs). Using flow cytometry and imaging techniques, we mapped the expression of activating Fc{gamma}Rs (CD64, CD32A, CD16A) and neonatal FcR (FcRn) under steady-state and stimulated conditions. We found that IFN-I selectively downregulates CD16A expression in classical monocytes while preserving other FcRs, whereas TAK-981 reduces FcRn expression in classical monocytes without affecting CD16A. Additionally, IFN-{beta} and TAK-981 but not IFN-2, selectively enhanced Fc{gamma}RI expression in moDC. IFN-{beta} also induced a stronger maturation and functional activation program in monocytes and moDCs compared with IFN-2, whereas TAK-981 largely reproduced the IFN-{beta}-driven phenotype and secretory profile. Furthermore, we demonstrated that IFN-I signaling alters the spatial distribution of FcRs, with IFN-{beta} and TAK-981 promoting distinct redistribution patterns of Fc{gamma}Rs in monocytes and moDCs. These findings reveal a novel layer of FcR regulation, highlighting that IFN-I and IFN inducers differentially modulate FcR expression, localization, and functional activation in a cell-type- and stimulus-specific manner. Overall, this work provides a framework for understanding how IFN-I-based immunotherapies may influence Fc-mediated immune functions while preserving FcRn-dependent antibody persistence.

candidates.title: C1q-mediated steric hindrance limits FcγR contribution to antibody-driven phagocytosis by human neutrophils
candidates.authors: Grönloh, M. L. B., de Vor, L., Zwarthoff, S. A., et al.
candidates.abstract: Phagocytosis and killing of bacteria by neutrophils is a key driver of human immunity against invading infections. IgG antibodies targeting the bacterial surface can potently enhance phagocytic uptake by engaging Fc gamma receptors (Fc{gamma}Rs) on the neutrophil membrane. In addition, IgG-mediated complement activation triggers surface deposition of complement opsonins that engage complement receptors (CRs) to further enhance target cell clearance. In this paper, we reveal that complement deposition prevents engagement of Fc{gamma}Rs to the Fc-domain of surface-bound IgG molecules. When complement is present, we observe that blockade of Fc{gamma}Rs does not influence phagocytosis of both Gram-positive and -negative bacteria (using Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae as model organisms). Complement-mediated hindrance of Fc{gamma}R engagement was observed in different model conditions, for example using either pre-existing polyclonal antibodies in human serum or recombinant monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting different bacterial antigens. Using Fc engineering, we found that inhibition of Fc{gamma}R binding is dependent on the ability of IgGs to form IgG hexamers. Mechanistically, we show that complement proteins, in particular C1q, directly prevents the interaction between IgG-Fc and Fc{gamma}R by steric hindrance. Together, these insights help us define the respective roles of Fc{gamma}R and CR in neutrophil phagocytosis, while also providing important fundamental insights for therapeutic antibody development.

candidates.title: Achieving near single-molecule sensitivity in separation-free protein detection using engineered kinetic proofreading
candidates.authors: Xuan, F., Fan, T. W., Chen, X., et al.
candidates.abstract: Unlike nucleic acids, proteins cannot be directly amplified. Ultrasensitive detection must therefore couple efficient analyte-to-signal conversion with strong suppression of target-independent background. Consistently detecting ~100 molecules (below which Poisson sampling noise alone causes CV to exceed 10%) across protein targets in a format as scalable and accessible as PCR remains unsolved. Separation-based ultrasensitive immunoassays require target binding stable enough to survive stringent washing and are therefore constrained by wash-induced signal loss and, more fundamentally, the relative scarcity of exceptionally tight binders. Performance consequently varies across targets; detection limits below 1,000 molecules remain rare. Conventional separation-free proximity assays avoid washing but incur background from random probe collisions, with reported detection limits frequently exceeding 100,000 molecules. Here we introduce Successive Proximity Extension Amplification Reaction (SPEAR), a separation-free architecture in which autonomous engineered DNA nanodevices emulate biological kinetic proofreading. Two successive irreversible proximity-extension steps compound discrimination between analyte-dependent and background reactions, suppressing spurious signals while preserving efficient analyte-to-signal conversion. This design reduces reliance on high-affinity binders and enables sub-fM detection from 1 uL samples through simple 3-step mixing followed by standard qPCR readout. Across 11 biomarkers tested, SPEAR consistently achieved sub-100-molecule detection limits. Where compared, it outperformed ultrasensitive separation-based platforms, analytically and clinically, including for low-abundance Alzheimer's disease biomarkers. SPEAR also precisely quantified SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibody titers from finger-prick dried blood spots, concordant with the cell-based reference assay on venous blood. It detected a distinct mixed phosphorylation state of Tau, and targeting this state resolved previously observed capillary-venous discordance and improved amyloid-status discrimination. These results establish engineered autonomous successive molecular discrimination as a practical strategy for near-single-molecule protein detection, extending the sensitivity, scalability and accessibility of PCR-based testing to non-amplifiable analytes.

candidates.title: The pharmacokinetics, bio-distribution and therapeutic efficacy of a trimeric nanobody against SARS-CoV-2 in the golden Syrian hamster COVID-19 model
candidates.authors: Sharma, P., Mega, D., Kirby, A., et al.
candidates.abstract: Nanobodies are promising medical countermeasures against respiratory viruses, but their local pharmacokinetics and therapeutic window remain incompletely defined. We evaluated the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution and efficacy of a SARS-CoV-2-neutralising trimeric nanobody (A8) in golden Syrian hamsters.
